activities.anchor: Heights ride along through vertical angles
activities.caption: call the height before the tangent does
activities.name: svTanEst

config.prompt: A target 50 m away is observed at +30° elevation. How far does it stand above the instrument's line of sight, in metres?
config.why: 50 × tan(30°) ≈ 28.87 m — heights ride on vertical angles, corrected afterwards for instrument height and, over long sights, Earth curvature.
config.context: North-south is the cosine direction, east-west the sine — and elevation is the tangent's turn.

activities.anchor: the classic field trick for finding
activities.caption: the classical repertoire — pair each method with its engine
activities.name: svClassMatch

config.prompt: Match each method to what it measures and fixes:

pairs.right: angles in triangles — one measured baseline, then the law of sines fixes every side
measured distances — the mirror-image method, via the law of cosines
fixes an unreachable point from angles only
standing at an unknown point, sighting three known ones — finding yourself

config.why: Depth perception is triangulation on a two-eye baseline, and astronomers pushed the same method to the stars — a good angle measurement goes a very long way.

config.text: Bookkeeping discipline: bearings converted consistently, coordinates carried forward leg by leg, and the interior angles of a closed traverse must total (n − %%0%%) × %%1%%° — a failure there means something worse than arithmetic happened.
config.hint: A triangle closes with 180°; every extra side adds another 180°.

activities.anchor: That square-root law is the most useful
activities.caption: call the misclosure before the quadrature does
activities.name: svMiscEst

config.prompt: Six traverse legs, each angle carrying 10 seconds of random error: the expected angular misclosure at closure is about how many seconds?
config.why: 10 × √6 ≈ 24.5″ — not 60 — because independent random errors partially cancel: roughly half the leg errors came back negative.
config.context: Shorten the legs at fixed leg count and the position error worsens: each angle error becomes position error proportional to leg length — long, well-conditioned legs beat many short ones.

activities.anchor: This is why instrument specifications quote angles
activities.caption: what does averaging buy? — which curve is real?
activities.name: svRepTrace

config.prompt: n repetitions of an angle reduce the random component by √n. Which curve is the random error against n?

curves.label: falling with the square root — quadrature
falling in direct proportion to n
not falling at all — averaging is useless

config.why: Independent errors add in quadrature: σ_R² = σ_a² + σ_b², so totals grow with the square root of the contributors — and turning angles face-left and face-right also cancels systematic collimation, procedure and statistics cooperating in one habit.

activities.caption: true or false — precision, accuracy, decimals
activities.name: svPrecJudge

statements.s: Precision is repeatability; accuracy is closeness to truth.
statements.why: They are different virtues — and a survey can have either without the other.

statements.s: A systematically short tape produces correct distances if you measure often enough.
statements.why: The systematic error has the same sign every time — repeat it a thousand times and it never averages out.

statements.s: More decimal places mean a better survey.
statements.why: The professional standard is a stated uncertainty that is defensible — the surveyor certifies how wrong the answer might be.

activities.anchor: A failure means find the blunder
activities.caption: the closure verdict — two ways to respond, drag the divider
activities.name: svCloseCompare

config.prompt: The traverse returns to its start and the numbers disagree. Drag the divider:

before.label: a failing misclosure
before.text: stop and hunt the mistake — adjusting around a failed closure certifies an error instead of finding it

after.label: a passing misclosure
after.text: distribute it honestly: angular spread equally among the angles, linear in proportion to leg length — the compass rule

config.why: The closure is compared against the specification (a boundary traverse might be held to 1 part in 10,000) before anything is finalised — the surveyor's receipt.

activities.anchor: the planet's shape enters the equations
activities.caption: one line of the geodesy brief is wrong — click it
activities.name: svGeoSpot

config.prompt: One line of this geodesy brief is wrong — click it:
lines: The Earth is modelled as an oblate ellipsoid — equatorial radius about 6,378 km, flattened by about 1 part in 298.
Meridians converge, so grid azimuths must be corrected to true north.
A conformal projection preserves distances everywhere, so UTM distances need no scale factor.
Ellipsoidal heights come free from GNSS; engineering and law use orthometric heights relative to the geoid.
The conversion is H = h − N, and the geoid undulates against the ellipsoid by tens of metres.
config.correction: A conformal projection preserves angles locally but imposes a small scale factor on distances — grid and ground differ by parts per hundred thousand, and professional work applies combined scale-and-height factors.
config.why: Flat-Earth arithmetic is not wrong — it is a local approximation, and the professional skill is knowing exactly where its validity ends.
